interview.question: What does `keyof` produce for a normal object type?
interview.answer: `keyof T` is a type-level query that produces the permitted property names of `T`. For `{ x: number; y: number }`, it is equivalent to `"x" | "y"`.
interview.followUp: How would you restrict a generic key to strings? Use `Extract<keyof T, string>` when the implementation cannot handle numeric or symbol keys.

interview.question: How is `keyof` used in a type-safe property accessor?
interview.answer: A generic parameter can be constrained with `K extends keyof T`, guaranteeing that `key` is valid for `obj`. Indexed access `T[K]` then represents the value type associated with that key.
interview.followUp: How can the same relationship type a setter? Declare `value: T[K]`, so the value must match the selected property’s type.

interview.question: How do index signatures affect `keyof`?
interview.answer: For a numeric index signature, `keyof` produces `number`. For a string index signature, it produces `string | number`, reflecting that numeric property access is coerced to a string in JavaScript.
interview.followUp: What happens with symbol-named properties? Modern TypeScript includes symbol-like property names in `keyof` results, so the result is not limited to strings and numbers.

keyPoints: For an object with explicitly declared properties, `keyof` creates a union of the corresponding key literals.
For `type Point = { x: number; y: number }`, `keyof Point` is equivalent to `"x" | "y"`.
Mapped types can iterate over a `keyof` result to derive a new type from every property.
For an intersection, the operator distributes over the constituents as a union of their key queries.
gotchas: Index signatures change the result from a finite literal-key union to an index-key type.
A string index signature also accounts for numeric access, so its result can be `string | number`.

lib.summary: The lib compiler option selects the JavaScript and environment API declarations available during type checking. Use it to align TypeScript's known APIs with the actual runtime, browser platform, and polyfills in a project.
lib.explanation: The lib compiler option controls which declaration files describe available JavaScript and environment APIs. It can replace the defaults inferred from target, letting a project include only the platform and ECMAScript features its runtime supplies, such as ES libraries, DOM types, or selected higher-level APIs.

parameters.name: compilerOptions.lib
parameters.description: An array of library names, such as "ES2020" or "DOM", that selects the declaration files included in the program.

lib.returns: No runtime return value; this is a tsconfig compiler option.

example.title: Selecting runtime API definitions
example.explanation: This configuration supplies type definitions for ES2020 APIs and browser DOM globals, allowing the file to use Map and document with type checking.

useCases.title: Exclude browser declarations
useCases.scenario: A Node or server project should not expose browser globals such as document and window to application code.

useCases.title: Describe browser APIs
useCases.scenario: A browser application needs DOM types alongside the ECMAScript APIs provided by its chosen runtime.

useCases.title: Model polyfilled APIs
useCases.scenario: A project uses polyfills or native runtime features that are newer than the syntax target.

useCases.title: Make environment assumptions explicit
useCases.scenario: A large codebase needs its declared platform surface to match a specific execution environment.

interview.question: What does TypeScript's lib option control?
interview.answer: The lib option selects declaration files for built-in JavaScript APIs and platform APIs. For example, ES2015 supplies APIs such as Promise, Map, Set, and Symbol, while DOM supplies browser globals such as window and document.
interview.followUp: How would you type-check browser APIs while emitting for an older JavaScript runtime? Set lib to include DOM and the required ECMAScript API declarations, then choose an appropriate lower target for emitted syntax.

interview.question: When should a project specify lib explicitly?
interview.answer: TypeScript normally chooses a default library set based partly on target. Explicit lib entries let a project remove unsuitable environment declarations, such as DOM types in a non-browser program, or add declarations for APIs supplied by polyfills.
interview.followUp: Why might lib include a newer ES library than target? Because a runtime or polyfill may provide those APIs even though the compiler still downlevels newer syntax.

interview.question: How are library choices represented?
interview.answer: lib entries name library groups rather than individual declaration filenames. The page lists high-level libraries such as ES5, ES2015, ES2016, and DOM, with aliases such as ES6 for ES2015 and ES7 for ES2016.
interview.followUp: What should you do if only part of a newer standard is available? Select the relevant granular library entries rather than claiming the entire higher-level standard library.

keyPoints: The option governs ambient declarations for standard JavaScript APIs, including core objects such as Math.
Browser-specific globals are separate from core JavaScript declarations; DOM is the documented library for APIs such as document.
The inferred library set follows target defaults, so raising target can make newer standard API types available automatically.
Server-side projects can omit DOM to prevent browser globals from appearing as valid ambient names.
A project can select declarations according to APIs supplied by its actual runtime or polyfills, independently of syntax support.
Library selection can model partial API availability instead of adopting every declaration from a complete ECMAScript level.
gotchas: Enabling noLib disables automatic library inclusion and takes precedence over lib.

Lowercase.summary: Lowercase<StringType> converts every character in a string type to its lowercase equivalent. Use it to derive normalized string-literal types, including names built with template literal types.
Lowercase.explanation: Lowercase is an intrinsic string manipulation type that transforms every character in a string type to its lowercase equivalent. It is especially useful inside template literal types when generating normalized names such as cache keys.

parameters.name: StringType
parameters.description: The string type whose characters should be converted to lowercase.

Lowercase.returns: A string type with every character converted to its lowercase equivalent.

example.title: Lowercase a string literal type
example.explanation: Transforms a string literal type into its lowercase form, allowing the compiler to check the normalized value.

useCases.title: Normalize literal types
useCases.scenario: Derive lowercase variants of string literal types for compile-time validation.

useCases.title: Generate cache-key types
useCases.scenario: Build prefixed identifiers whose input portion must use lowercase casing.

useCases.title: Encode naming rules
useCases.scenario: Enforce naming conventions in generic template literal types.

interview.question: What does Lowercase do?
interview.answer: Lowercase<StringType> is an intrinsic string manipulation type. It converts each character in the supplied string type to its lowercase equivalent.
interview.followUp: How can it be used with a generic? Define a constraint such as `Str extends string`, then use `Lowercase<Str>` inside a template literal type to construct a normalized result.

interview.question: How does Lowercase work with template literal types?
interview.answer: It can be embedded in a template literal type to derive a new string literal type. For example, `id-${Lowercase<"MY_APP">}` produces `"id-my_app"`.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful in large codebases? It lets APIs encode naming conventions in types, so inconsistent casing becomes a compile-time error.

interview.question: How does Lowercase differ from related casing utilities?
interview.answer: The type parameter represents the input string type, and the result is the same string with every character converted to lowercase. TypeScript includes it as a built-in compiler intrinsic for performance.
interview.followUp: What related utilities exist? `Uppercase` transforms every character to uppercase, while `Capitalize` and `Uncapitalize` affect only the first character.

keyPoints: Lowercase belongs to TypeScript’s built-in family of string manipulation types.
The transformation applies to every character rather than only the first one.
For a string literal input, the compiler evaluates the resulting lowercase literal type.
Combining a prefix with a lowercased input can produce a predictable cache-key type.
gotchas: Lowercase is compiler-provided rather than a type alias declared in the standard declaration files, so searching `.d.ts` files for its implementation will not find one.

Mapped Types.summary: Mapped types transform an existing type by iterating over a union of property keys, commonly keyof another type. They can change property values, modifiers, and—using key remapping—property names.
Mapped Types.explanation: A mapped type creates a new type by iterating over a key union, commonly obtained with keyof, and assigning a transformed property type to each key. The mapped declaration can also preserve, add, remove, or conditionally rename properties while retaining their relationship to the source type.

parameters.name: Type
parameters.description: The source type whose keys and property types are transformed.

Mapped Types.returns: A new object type whose properties are produced by iterating over the selected keys.

example.title: Map feature members to flags
example.explanation: The mapped type transforms every property in Features into a boolean property.

useCases.title: Generate boolean flags
useCases.scenario: Create a configuration type whose entries indicate whether corresponding features are enabled.

useCases.title: Change optionality
useCases.scenario: Derive an editable or required variant without duplicating every property declaration.

useCases.title: Remap and filter keys
useCases.scenario: Generate renamed properties or omit selected members while deriving an API surface.

interview.question: What is a mapped type, and what does keyof commonly contribute?
interview.answer: A mapped type iterates over a union of PropertyKey values, often keyof Type, and creates one output property per key. Its value expression can transform each source property, such as changing every value to boolean.
interview.followUp: How can a mapped type remove selected properties? Use key remapping with an as clause and produce never for keys that should be excluded.

interview.question: How do mapped types control readonly and optional properties?
interview.answer: The modifiers are readonly and ?. A modifier without a prefix means +, while - removes the corresponding modifier, for example -? makes mapped properties required.
interview.followUp: How would you make every property mutable and required? Apply -readonly and -? in the mapped declaration.

interview.question: How do key remapping and filtering work?
interview.answer: An as clause remaps each source key to a new key type. Conditional logic can return never to filter a key, and template literal types can derive names from existing keys.
interview.followUp: What constraint is useful when remapping only string keys? A conditional such as Key extends string ? ... : never excludes number and symbol keys.

keyPoints: Mapped types iterate over a key union and construct a related output type.
keyof is a common way to obtain the source type's property-key union.
A mapped value expression can uniformly replace every source property's value type.
Mapped declarations can control mutability and optionality in addition to value types.
The plus modifier is implicit, so an unprefixed readonly or optional marker adds that modifier.
Mapped types can iterate over unions beyond the usual property-key union in supported transformations.
gotchas: Mapped properties may carry readonly and optional modifiers; use + or - prefixes when you need to explicitly add or remove those modifiers.
Key remapping is available through an as clause, so the output keys need not be identical to the input keys.
A remapped key of never removes that property from the resulting type.

MethodDecorator.summary: A legacy method decorator is placed before a method and receives its target, name, and property descriptor at runtime. It can observe, modify, or replace the method definition.
MethodDecorator.explanation: A legacy method decorator is placed immediately before a method and receives the class prototype for an instance method, the member name, and its property descriptor. It can inspect the method, alter the descriptor, or replace the method definition by returning a descriptor.
MethodDecorator.syntax: function methodDecorator(target: object, propertyKey: string | symbol, descriptor: PropertyDescriptor): PropertyDescriptor | void

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The class constructor for a static method, or the class prototype for an instance method.

parameters.name: propertyKey
parameters.description: The name of the decorated method.

parameters.name: descriptor
parameters.description: The method's property descriptor; a decorator can inspect or modify it.

MethodDecorator.returns: A PropertyDescriptor optionally returned to install a replacement method definition; the decorator may also modify the supplied descriptor in place.

example.title: Wrapping an instance method
example.explanation: The decorator wraps the method implementation through its property descriptor, logs each call, and preserves the returned value.

useCases.title: Instrumentation
useCases.scenario: Add tracing, timing, or audit output around method calls without editing each method body.

useCases.title: Behavior substitution
useCases.scenario: Replace or wrap a method implementation while preserving the decorated class API.

useCases.title: Cross-cutting method policies
useCases.scenario: Inspect descriptor information to enforce conventions or attach method-level behavior.

interview.question: What arguments does a legacy method decorator receive?
interview.answer: A method decorator is declared immediately before a method. At runtime, its function receives the class constructor for a static method or the prototype for an instance method, followed by the member name and property descriptor.
interview.followUp: How can it change behavior? Modify the descriptor, commonly by replacing descriptor.value, or return a property descriptor that installs a replacement definition.

interview.question: What can a method decorator do?
interview.answer: It can observe, modify, or replace the method definition because it operates on the method's property descriptor. A wrapper can replace descriptor.value and delegate to the original implementation.
interview.followUp: What must be preserved in a wrapper? Preserve the receiver and arguments when forwarding, and return the original result when the wrapper is intended to be transparent.

interview.question: What is the relevant decorator application order?
interview.answer: For instance members, decorators on parameters are applied before method, accessor, or property decorators for that member. Static-member decorators are processed afterward, followed by constructor parameter decorators and then the class decorator.
interview.followUp: Why does ordering matter? Multiple decorators can observe or transform the same declaration, so their application order affects which descriptor or definition each decorator receives.

keyPoints: Place the decorator directly before the method declaration.
The legacy API centers on the method's PropertyDescriptor, which provides access to its definition.
Use a method decorator for observation, descriptor changes, or replacement of the method.
The first runtime argument identifies whether the decorated method belongs to the class itself or its prototype.
The second runtime argument is the decorated member's name.
The third runtime argument is the member's property descriptor.
gotchas: Do not apply a method decorator to declaration files, overload signatures, or ambient declarations such as declare classes.
This legacy decorator form requires the experimentalDecorators compiler option.

module.summary: A TypeScript file with a top-level import or export is a module; a file without either is a script. Modules have their own scope, while scripts contribute declarations to the global scope.
module.explanation: TypeScript treats a file with a top-level import or export as a module. That file has its own scope, so its declarations are not placed in the global scope; files without top-level imports or exports are scripts instead.

example.title: A minimal TypeScript module
example.explanation: A file with a top-level export is a module, and another module can import its exported binding.

useCases.title: Explicit dependencies
useCases.scenario: Organize application code into files with explicit imports and exports.

useCases.title: Scope isolation
useCases.scenario: Prevent unrelated files from sharing names through the global scope.

useCases.title: Controlled exports
useCases.scenario: Expose only selected APIs from an implementation file.

interview.question: How does TypeScript decide whether a file is a module?
interview.answer: A TypeScript file is a module when it contains a top-level import or export. Otherwise, TypeScript treats it as a script, whose contents are available in the global scope.
interview.followUp: How do you make a file a module when it has no runtime imports or exports? Add an explicit type-only import or export, such as `export {}`.

interview.question: Why are modules useful in a large codebase?
interview.answer: Module scope prevents declarations from being shared through the global scope. Files can expose selected bindings through exports and consume them through imports.
interview.followUp: What is the practical benefit in a large codebase? Explicit dependency boundaries reduce accidental name collisions and make relationships easier for tooling to analyze.

interview.question: Is module status the same as the emitted module format?
interview.answer: The module concept follows ECMAScript 2015: top-level `import` and `export` determine module status. This is separate from the particular runtime module format used when JavaScript is emitted.
interview.followUp: Which compiler setting addresses emitted format? The `module` compiler option controls the module format of emitted JavaScript and also informs related module analysis.

keyPoints: A top-level `import` or `export` is enough to classify the file as a module.
Without a top-level import or export, the file is classified as a script.
Module execution uses a private scope instead of the global scope.
TypeScript uses the ECMAScript 2015 module classification rule.
gotchas: A file containing no top-level import or export is a script, so its declarations are globally visible rather than module-scoped.
Module declarations do not automatically become global names; each module executes in its own scope.

Module Augmentation.summary: Module augmentation lets a module add type declarations to an existing module's named exports. The declarations merge with the original API, while any runtime patch must be implemented and loaded separately.
Module Augmentation.explanation: A module augmentation reopens an existing module with declare module and adds declarations that merge with its original named exports. The augmentation changes TypeScript's view of the module; runtime behavior still requires an implementation, usually installed by importing a patch module.

parameters.name: module specifier
parameters.description: The module specifier naming the existing module whose declarations will be extended.

parameters.name: augmentation body
parameters.description: Existing named declarations to merge into the target module.

Module Augmentation.returns: The augmentation contributes merged type declarations to the named exports of an existing module; it does not itself produce a runtime value.

example.title: Augmenting an Observable module
example.explanation: The augmentation adds the map method to Observable's type, while the imported patch supplies its runtime implementation.

useCases.title: Extend a third-party API
useCases.scenario: A library exposes a class or interface that application code needs to extend with project-specific members.

useCases.title: Describe a runtime patch
useCases.scenario: A separate JavaScript file adds a method to an imported class prototype.

useCases.title: Augment global scope
useCases.scenario: A module needs to add members to global types from within module code.

interview.question: How does module augmentation work?
interview.answer: Use declare module with the target module specifier, then write compatible declarations inside it. TypeScript merges those declarations with the original module as though they were declared in the same file.
interview.followUp: Can the augmentation add a new exported function? No. It can only patch an existing declaration, not add a new top-level declaration.

interview.question: Does module augmentation implement the added behavior?
interview.answer: The augmentation supplies type information only. If the added method or property must work at runtime, code must also patch the actual object or prototype, and consumers must load that patch.
interview.followUp: Why might a type-checking example still fail at runtime? The declaration merge does not create JavaScript; the implementation module must be executed.

interview.question: What export limitation applies?
interview.answer: Only named exports can be augmented. Default exports cannot be addressed by exported name because default is reserved, so they are excluded by this feature.
interview.followUp: What design alternative helps extensibility? Expose a named class, interface, or function that consumers can augment instead of relying on a default export.

keyPoints: The compiler combines augmentation declarations with the target module's declarations, giving consumers the extended type.
Runtime extension is achieved separately by importing the object and modifying it, such as adding a prototype method.
The declaration uses ambient-module syntax: declare module followed by the module specifier and an augmentation body.
Resolution uses the same rules as ordinary module references, so the specifier must identify the existing module.
gotchas: An augmentation cannot introduce a new top-level export; it may only modify declarations that already exist in the target module.
Default exports cannot be augmented, so design the target API around named exports when extension is required.
The string in declare module follows normal import/export module-specifier resolution; an incorrect specifier targets nothing useful.

moduleResolution.summary: `moduleResolution` chooses how TypeScript maps import, export, and require specifiers to files. Configure it to match the target runtime or bundler, such as `nodenext` for modern Node.js or `bundler` for bundler-managed projects.
moduleResolution.explanation: `moduleResolution` selects the algorithm TypeScript uses to turn module specifiers from imports, exports, or require calls into files. Choose a mode that matches the runtime or bundler: `node16`/`nodenext` for modern Node.js, `bundler` for bundlers, and `node10` only for older CommonJS environments.

parameters.name: moduleResolution
parameters.description: Resolution strategy used to locate files for module specifiers. Current documented choices include `node16`, `nodenext`, `node10`, `bundler`, and `classic`.

moduleResolution.returns: No runtime return value; this compiler option changes how TypeScript resolves modules.

example.title: Use NodeNext module resolution
example.explanation: Use Node's modern resolution rules for a Node.js project so TypeScript models the runtime's import and require behavior.

useCases.title: Model modern Node.js resolution
useCases.scenario: A project runs directly on current Node.js and may use both ESM imports and CommonJS require.

useCases.title: Match bundler behavior
useCases.scenario: A web application is resolved and emitted by a bundler.

useCases.title: Support legacy Node.js
useCases.scenario: A legacy application targets an older Node.js CommonJS environment.

interview.question: What does `moduleResolution` control?
interview.answer: It determines how TypeScript resolves module specifiers to files. The setting should match the module-resolution behavior of the target runtime or bundler.
interview.followUp: How would you choose it for a bundled web application versus a Node.js application? Use `bundler` for the former and `nodenext` or `node16` for the latter, paired with the corresponding `module` setting.

interview.question: Which strategy is appropriate for modern Node.js?
interview.answer: Use `node16` or `nodenext` for modern Node.js. These modes account for Node.js supporting both ECMAScript imports and CommonJS `require`, which use different resolution algorithms.
interview.followUp: Why must the `module` option also matter? The emitted form determines whether Node.js applies import or require resolution, so the paired settings let TypeScript select the appropriate algorithm.

interview.question: How does `bundler` differ from Node.js resolution?
interview.answer: Use `bundler` when a bundler performs resolution. It supports package `imports` and `exports` while allowing extensionless relative imports, unlike Node.js resolution modes.
interview.followUp: What compatibility issue can this create? Code accepted by `bundler` may fail when executed directly by Node.js because Node.js can require extensions on relative imports.

keyPoints: The option maps strings in import, export, and require statements to files on disk.
Treat the runtime or bundler as the source of truth when selecting a resolution strategy.
Modern Node.js projects generally use node16 or nodenext.
Select bundler when a bundler, rather than Node.js directly, resolves application modules.
Bundler, node16, and nodenext understand package entry-point and internal-import maps.
When runtime-style lookup points at JavaScript, TypeScript substitutes a corresponding TypeScript source or declaration file first.
gotchas: Node16 and NodeNext must be paired with corresponding module settings so resolution reflects whether emitted code uses import or require.
Bundler mode accepts extensionless relative imports, so code that works there may not satisfy Node.js's stricter import rules.
Avoid node10 for new projects; it models older Node.js CommonJS behavior.
Do not choose the classic strategy for current projects.

never.summary: `never` represents impossible values and unreachable execution paths. It is especially useful for exhaustive checking of narrowed unions and for functions that throw or never terminate.
never.explanation: `never` describes an impossible value or an execution path that cannot complete normally. Use it for functions that always throw or terminate, and as an exhaustiveness check after narrowing a union.
never.syntax:
type never
function assertNever(value: never): never

example.title: Exhaustive discriminated-union handling
example.explanation: The default branch is accepted only when narrowing has removed every valid Shape variant.

useCases.title: Non-returning functions
useCases.scenario: A function always throws or terminates without returning.

useCases.title: Exhaustiveness checking
useCases.scenario: A discriminated union is handled in a switch statement.

useCases.title: Type-level filtering
useCases.scenario: A conditional type needs a fallback for unsupported inputs.

interview.question: What does the `never` type represent?
interview.answer: `never` represents a value that cannot occur. In a return position, it indicates that a function throws or terminates execution rather than producing a value.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from `void`? `void` describes a function whose result is not useful or has no value, whereas `never` means normal completion cannot happen.

interview.question: How can `never` enforce exhaustive switch handling?
interview.answer: After narrowing removes every member of a union, TypeScript uses `never` for the remaining impossible state. Assigning that state to a `never` parameter lets a default branch verify that all cases were handled.
interview.followUp: What happens when a union gains a new variant? The default branch’s argument is no longer `never`, so the compiler reports the missing case.

interview.question: What are the assignability rules for `never`?
interview.answer: `never` is assignable to every type, but no other type is assignable to it except `never` itself. This makes it suitable as the parameter type of an assertion function used at an unreachable branch.
interview.followUp: Why can an assertion function return `never` too? Because it throws or otherwise never reaches its caller, so the call expression itself has an impossible continuation.

keyPoints: Control-flow narrowing can reduce a discriminated union to an impossible branch represented by `never`.
A `never` check in a switch default branch catches newly added union members at compile time.
Its one-way assignability makes `never` safe as the required type for an impossible state.
gotchas: A value cannot normally be assigned to `never`; the intended direction is that `never` can be assigned to other types.
A union containing `never` usually simplifies to its other members, so `never` may disappear from displayed or inferred union types.

noImplicitAny.summary: noImplicitAny makes TypeScript report errors when it would infer any because a value lacks an annotation or usable contextual type. Enable it in compilerOptions to prevent accidental loss of type checking.
noImplicitAny.explanation: Enable this compiler option to make TypeScript report locations where it would otherwise infer the type any. In large codebases, annotate those values or provide enough contextual typing to preserve static checking instead of silently accepting unchecked operations.

parameters.name: noImplicitAny
parameters.description: Boolean compiler option. When true, reports declarations and expressions whose type would otherwise be inferred as any.

example.title: Enable noImplicitAny
example.explanation: With noImplicitAny enabled, the unannotated parameter causes a compile-time error; add an explicit type to make the function valid.

useCases.title: Prevent accidental implicit any
useCases.scenario: Enforce explicit types for unannotated parameters and declarations in new modules.

useCases.title: Catch hidden type errors
useCases.scenario: Detect unchecked member access that would otherwise compile through an inferred any.

useCases.title: Improve large-codebase safety
useCases.scenario: Adopt stronger checking incrementally by enabling the option in a project configuration.

interview.question: What does noImplicitAny do?
interview.answer: It reports an error whenever TypeScript would infer any because no annotation or contextual type determines the value's type. This prevents unchecked operations from passing silently.
interview.followUp: How can a project enable the related strictness settings together? Set strict to true, then opt out of individual strictness flags when necessary.

interview.question: What is a typical diagnostic caused by noImplicitAny?
interview.answer: A parameter such as function fn(s) can receive an implicit any error when TypeScript cannot infer s. Giving s an explicit type resolves that diagnostic and restores checking for operations on it.
interview.followUp: What happens if the parameter is explicitly declared as any? The explicit annotation is intentional and is not an implicit-any inference diagnostic.

interview.question: How do you enable noImplicitAny?
interview.answer: The setting belongs in compilerOptions in tsconfig.json, where it can be enabled with a boolean value. It can also be enabled through the corresponding compiler command-line option.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful in a large codebase? It turns accidental loss of type information into an actionable compile-time error.

keyPoints: The option addresses cases where missing annotations leave TypeScript unable to infer a more specific type.
Implicit any can hide invalid member access and other mistakes because the unchecked value accepts operations that a known type would reject.
Enabling the flag converts an otherwise silent fallback into a compiler diagnostic.
The diagnostic identifies the specific declaration whose type was not inferred.
The setting is a compiler flag and is enabled in project configuration under compilerOptions.
gotchas: The option reports implicit any in places where inference cannot determine a type; an untyped function parameter is a common example.
An explicitly written any is different from an implicit any; this option targets the latter.

NoInfer.summary: NoInfer<Type> blocks inference from the wrapped type while remaining identical to Type for other purposes. Use it when one generic argument should establish a type and another should only be checked against it.
NoInfer.explanation: NoInfer<T> keeps TypeScript from using the wrapped type position as an inference source. The wrapped type otherwise behaves like T, so it still participates in checking after inference is determined elsewhere.

parameters.name: Type
parameters.description: The type to use while suppressing inference from the wrapped position.

example.explanation: The first argument determines the allowed color union, while NoInfer prevents the optional default color from expanding that union.

useCases.title: Validate defaults
useCases.scenario: A collection and a default value share a generic type, but only the collection should determine that type.

useCases.title: Control inference sources
useCases.scenario: Several arguments can contribute incompatible candidates to a generic type parameter.

useCases.title: Protect literal unions
useCases.scenario: An API should preserve a narrow inferred union instead of widening it from a later argument.

interview.question: What is NoInfer<T>?
interview.answer: NoInfer<T> is a utility type released in TypeScript 5.4. It blocks inference into T, while remaining identical to T for other type-checking purposes.
interview.followUp: What problem does it solve in a generic function? It lets one argument establish the generic type and makes another argument conform to that established type instead of widening it.

interview.question: How does NoInfer affect generic inference?
interview.answer: In a generic function with multiple candidate sources, TypeScript normally infers from values passed to those positions. Wrapping one position in NoInfer prevents that position from contributing inference candidates.
interview.followUp: How would you use it for a default value? Infer the element union from the collection parameter, then write the default parameter as NoInfer<C>.

interview.question: Why is NoInfer useful in the createStreetLight example?
interview.answer: For a street-light helper, C can be inferred from the colors array, while NoInfer<C> on defaultColor requires the default to belong to that inferred union. An invalid default therefore produces an assignability error.
interview.followUp: What happens without NoInfer? The default argument may become an additional inference source, allowing an unintended value to influence C.

keyPoints: NoInfer<T> prevents inference from the type argument position it wraps.
After inference, the wrapped type has the same type-checking meaning as the unwrapped type.
The utility became part of TypeScript in version 5.4.
Without an inference barrier, multiple function arguments can supply candidates for a generic type.
NoInfer stops TypeScript from searching inside the wrapped type for inference candidates.
A value rejected by the inferred union produces a normal assignability diagnostic at the call site.
gotchas: NoInfer does not create a different runtime or checking type; its special behavior is limited to inference.
Apply NoInfer at the position whose values should be validated against an inference established from another argument.

NonNullable.explanation: NonNullable<Type> transforms a type by removing null and undefined from it. Applied to a union, it preserves the remaining members, making it useful for representing values after validation or other checks.

noUncheckedIndexedAccess.summary: The noUncheckedIndexedAccess compiler option adds undefined to undeclared indexed properties and array element reads. This makes missing keys and out-of-bounds access visible to the type checker.
noUncheckedIndexedAccess.explanation: Enable this compiler option when index signatures or array lookups may refer to missing entries. TypeScript adds undefined to undeclared indexed properties and array elements, requiring a guard or another explicit handling strategy before those values are used.

example.explanation: With the option enabled, an undeclared indexed property can be undefined, so the code narrows it before use.

useCases.title: Validate dictionary lookups
useCases.scenario: An object has a string index signature but only some keys are populated.

useCases.title: Detect possible out-of-bounds reads
useCases.scenario: Code reads arrays by calculated positions or loops over uncertain bounds.

useCases.title: Strengthen lookup safety
useCases.scenario: A large codebase wants compiler feedback for missing indexed values.

interview.question: What does noUncheckedIndexedAccess change for index signatures?
interview.answer: It changes the type of an undeclared property accessed through an index signature by adding undefined. A declared property such as env.NAME keeps its declared string type, while env.NODE_ENV becomes string | undefined.
interview.followUp: What happens with arrays? Array indexing is checked more strictly too, so an element read can include undefined even inside a bounds-checked loop.

interview.question: Why is this option not enabled by strict?
interview.answer: The option is not included by strict because it can produce noisy diagnostics in codebases that use broad index signatures. Teams should enable it deliberately and assess whether the additional checks fit their code.
interview.followUp: How should code handle a possibly missing value? Narrow it with an existence check, or use a non-null assertion only when the invariant is guaranteed elsewhere.

interview.question: What kinds of bugs can this option catch?
interview.answer: It helps catch out-of-bounds array access and missing keys represented by an index signature. The compiler models those reads as potentially undefined rather than assuming every lookup succeeds.
interview.followUp: Does it change explicitly declared keys? No: declared properties retain their declared types; the added undefined applies to undeclared indexed fields and indexed element reads.

keyPoints: An indexed property not explicitly declared in the type is treated as possibly absent.
The option affects both property-style and bracket-style access when the accessed member is not known to exist.
Array element reads receive the same missing-value scrutiny, helping reveal possible out-of-bounds access.
A practical benefit is detecting array lookups that may exceed the valid range.
gotchas: Turning on this option can expose many new errors, because strict does not enable it automatically.
A non-null assertion suppresses the diagnostic without proving that the property exists, so an existence check is safer when absence is possible.

number.summary: A number type alias assigns a domain-specific name to TypeScript’s existing `number` type. It improves readability but does not create a distinct or nominal numeric type.
number.explanation: A type alias gives the existing number type another name; it does not create a distinct type. Values typed with the alias have the same assignability and behavior as values typed directly as number, so the alias is mainly useful for domain terminology or consistent declarations in a large codebase.

example.explanation: The alias documents that these values are numbers while preserving the original number type.

useCases.scenario: Use a meaningful name such as `DurationSeconds` or `RetryCount` when a codebase repeatedly passes numbers with a specific domain meaning.

useCases.title: Standardize repeated annotations
useCases.scenario: Give a shared numeric concept one canonical name across function parameters, return types, and object properties.

useCases.title: Name library-facing values
useCases.scenario: Expose a public API using a stable domain term while retaining ordinary number assignability.

interview.question: What does a number type alias create?
interview.answer: A type alias such as `type NumberValue = number` introduces an alternate name for the existing `number` type. It does not create a new nominal type, so `NumberValue` and `number` are assignable in the same way.
interview.followUp: How would you model a union instead? Use a type alias such as `type Result = number | string`; aliases can name unions as well as primitives.

interview.question: When is a primitive alias useful?
interview.answer: It can make a repeated primitive clearer by expressing domain intent, such as `type DurationSeconds = number`. The compiler still treats the alias as number, so it does not validate units or distinguish durations from other numbers.
interview.followUp: How can stronger distinction be added? Use a branded or otherwise structurally distinctive type pattern rather than a plain primitive alias.

interview.question: What kinds of types can aliases name?
interview.answer: Type aliases can name primitives, unions, tuples, object types, and other types that would otherwise be written directly. For a plain number alias, the declaration is `type Name = number;`.
interview.followUp: Can a type alias be generic? Yes; the documentation shows aliases with type parameters, such as `type Container<T> = { value: T }`.

keyPoints: Declare the alias with the `type` keyword followed by an identifier, an equals sign, and the aliased type.
The basic declaration for this card is `type Second = number;`, which names the built-in numeric type.
Unlike an interface, a type alias can directly name a primitive such as number, as well as composite forms.
A value annotated directly as number demonstrates the underlying type represented by the alias.
A value annotated with the alias accepts numeric values just as the direct number annotation does.
gotchas: A number alias does not enforce a separate numeric domain or add nominal safety; it primarily documents intent.
Do not use a number alias when distinct, non-interchangeable types are required; the alias remains interchangeable with number.

object.summary: A type alias names a TypeScript type, commonly an object shape with typed properties. It improves reuse and readability without creating a distinct runtime or nominal type.
object.explanation: A type alias gives a name to a type, including an object type described by named properties and their types. The alias is only another name for that type, so using it is equivalent to writing the underlying structure directly; aliases can also be generic and can represent unions, primitives, and other types.

Choose an alias when the reusable abstraction may need to express non-object types or generic helper types.
gotchas: A type alias does not create a nominal or distinct type; it only names the existing type.
Omitting a property type causes it to be inferred as any, so explicit property types are generally safer.

Omit.summary: Omit<Type, Keys> creates a new type with all properties from Type except the keys listed in Keys. It is globally available and complements Pick.
Omit.explanation: Omit constructs a new object type from an existing type by retaining every property except the keys specified in its second type argument. The keys can be a string literal or a union of string literals, making it useful for deriving variants without repeating the original declaration.

interview.question: What does Omit do, and what can its Keys argument contain?
interview.answer: Omit<Type, Keys> creates a type containing all properties from Type except those listed by Keys. Keys may be one string literal or a union of string literals.
interview.followUp: How does it relate to Pick? Pick keeps only selected properties, while Omit removes selected properties from the complete property set.

interview.question: Why use Omit instead of redefining a similar object type?
interview.answer: Omit is a globally available TypeScript utility type. It is useful when a derived type should preserve the source shape except for a small block-listed set of properties.
interview.followUp: What is a common alternative when the desired result is an allow-list? Use Pick with the properties that should remain.

interview.question: When was Omit introduced and how is it parameterized?
interview.answer: The utility was released in TypeScript 3.5. Its declaration is generic: the first parameter supplies the source type and the second supplies the keys to remove.
interview.followUp: What happens if several keys must be excluded? Pass a union of string literal keys as the second argument.

keyPoints: It derives a new type by retaining the source type's properties and excluding the specified keys.
The keys argument accepts one property name or a union of property-name literals.
No import is needed because Omit is provided as a global utility type.
Omit is the complementary operation to Pick: it expresses exclusion rather than selection.
gotchas: Omit removes named properties, whereas Pick selects only the named properties.

OmitThisParameter.summary: `OmitThisParameter<Type>` removes an explicit `this` parameter from a function type. Functions without an explicit `this` remain unchanged, while generic information and all but the final overload are not preserved.
OmitThisParameter.explanation: `OmitThisParameter<Type>` transforms a function type that declares an explicit `this` parameter into an equivalent callable type without that parameter. If the source function has no explicit `this`, it remains unchanged; when overloads or generics are present, only the final overload is retained and generic parameters are discarded.

parameters.description: The function type whose explicit `this` parameter should be removed.

interview.question: What does OmitThisParameter do?
interview.answer: It removes an explicitly declared `this` parameter from a function type. If no explicit `this` exists, the original type is returned unchanged.
interview.followUp: What happens to an overloaded generic function? Only its last overload is propagated, and its generics are erased.

interview.question: How does it affect function calls?
interview.answer: The resulting type is callable without a `this` argument, while ordinary parameters remain unchanged. This is useful when exposing a method as a standalone callback.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve the receiver instead? Keep the original function type, or use a type that explicitly includes its `this` parameter.

interview.question: What is the syntax and input?
interview.answer: It is a standard utility type with one type argument: `OmitThisParameter<Type>`. The argument is the function type from which the explicit receiver parameter should be removed.
interview.followUp: What if the input is not declared with `this`? The utility leaves that type unchanged.

keyPoints: The utility transforms a function type by removing its explicit receiver parameter.
A function without an explicit `this` annotation passes through without a type change.
For an annotated receiver, TypeScript creates a new callable function type rather than mutating the original.
Generic information is discarded, and overloaded inputs contribute only their final signature.
The utility was introduced in TypeScript 3.3.
gotchas: Applying this utility to a generic or overloaded function type loses its generic parameters and preserves only the last overload.

override.summary: `override` marks a derived-class member as an intentional replacement for an inherited member. TypeScript verifies that the base class contains a matching member, while `noImplicitOverride` can require the annotation across a codebase.
override.explanation: The `override` modifier marks a class member as an intentional replacement for a member inherited from a base class. TypeScript checks that a corresponding member exists in the base class, and `noImplicitOverride` can require this modifier for every overriding member.
override.returns: The overridden member's declared return type; `override` itself produces no runtime value.

interview.question: What does the `override` modifier do?
interview.answer: `override` documents and verifies that a derived-class member replaces a member from its base class. TypeScript reports an error if no same-named member exists in the base class.
interview.followUp: How can a codebase require the modifier consistently? Enable `noImplicitOverride`; then every superclass override must explicitly use `override`.

interview.question: Why is `override` useful during refactoring?
interview.answer: The modifier protects against accidental divergence when a base member is renamed. If the derived member is not updated, TypeScript can detect that the claimed override no longer matches.
interview.followUp: What configuration complements the modifier? `noImplicitOverride` turns implicit overrides into errors, making the intent explicit throughout the hierarchy.

interview.question: When was `override` introduced, and what option is associated with it?
interview.answer: TypeScript 4.3 introduced `override` together with the `noImplicitOverride` option. The modifier applies to members such as methods that are intended to replace inherited members.
interview.followUp: What happens if a derived method is merely intended to be new? Leave off `override`; adding it would cause an error unless the base class declares a matching member.

keyPoints: The modifier was introduced in TypeScript 4.3.
A marked method must correspond to a same-named member in the base class.
The compiler option complements explicit override annotations.
gotchas: An `override` modifier is invalid when the base class has no member with the same name.
With `noImplicitOverride`, omitting `override` from an overriding member is an error.

ParameterDecorator.summary: A parameter decorator is a runtime callback placed before a parameter in a class constructor or method. It receives the owning target, member name, and parameter index, and is primarily used to observe or record parameter metadata.
ParameterDecorator.explanation: A parameter decorator is placed immediately before a parameter in a class constructor or method. At runtime, TypeScript invokes it with the relevant constructor or prototype, the member name, and the parameter’s zero-based position; its return value is discarded, so it observes or records information rather than directly replacing the parameter.

interview.question: What is a parameter decorator and what arguments does it receive?
interview.answer: A parameter decorator is written immediately before a parameter in a class constructor or method. Its runtime callback receives the constructor or prototype, the member name, and the parameter’s ordinal index.
interview.followUp: What can it change? It cannot directly replace the parameter or method: the decorator is observational, and its return value is ignored.

interview.question: How does the target differ for static and instance members?
interview.answer: For a static member, the first argument is the class constructor; for an instance member, it is the class prototype. The second argument identifies the member, and the third is the parameter’s position in the parameter list.
interview.followUp: Why does the first argument differ? Static members belong to the constructor, whereas instance members belong to the prototype.

interview.question: Are parameter decorators supported by TypeScript’s standard decorators?
interview.answer: The documented legacy parameter-decorator form uses the experimental decorators model and is distinct from the newer standard decorators proposal. TypeScript 5.0’s standard decorators do not support parameter decoration.
interview.followUp: What compatibility issue follows? Code using parameter decorators must use the legacy experimental-decorator support rather than the standard decorator implementation.

keyPoints: Place the decorator directly before the method or constructor parameter it annotates.
It applies to parameters belonging to class constructors or class methods.
The target identifies the owning constructor for static members or prototype for instance members.
The callback receives the decorated method or constructor member name.
The index identifies which parameter was decorated, using its position in the declaration.
The decorator expression resolves to a function that runs during class definition.
gotchas: It cannot transform the parameter or alter the method directly; use it for observation or metadata-style recording.
Do not place parameter decorators in .d.ts files, overload signatures, or declare-based ambient declarations.
Returning a replacement function or other value has no effect.

Parameters.explanation: Parameters<Type> evaluates a function type's parameter list as a tuple. Applying it to a function declaration via typeof preserves the parameter names and optionality represented by that function type; for overloaded functions, TypeScript uses the last signature.

Partial.summary: Partial<Type> constructs a type with every property of Type made optional. It represents any subset of the original type and is commonly used for partial updates.
Partial.explanation: Partial<T> creates a type whose properties correspond to T, but each property is optional. It is useful when an operation accepts a subset of an existing object’s fields, such as a patch or update function, while preserving each field’s original value type.

interview.question: What does Partial<T> do?
interview.answer: Partial<T> is a global utility type that makes every property in T optional. The resulting type represents all subsets of T while retaining each property’s original type.
interview.followUp: How can its transformation be expressed? A mapped type equivalent is `{ [P in keyof T]?: T[P] }`.

interview.question: When is Partial<T> useful?
interview.answer: Use Partial<T> for APIs that update only selected fields of an existing object. For example, an update function can accept `Partial<Todo>` while merging those fields into a complete Todo.
interview.followUp: How would you require at least one update field? Define a separate mapped or union type that makes one key required; Partial<T> alone also allows `{}`.

interview.question: When was Partial introduced, and where is it available?
interview.answer: Partial<T> was released in TypeScript 2.1 and is included globally in the standard library. It is one of TypeScript’s built-in utility types.
interview.followUp: What related transformation makes properties immutable instead? `Readonly<T>` preserves the property set while preventing assignment through the resulting type.

keyPoints: The type preserves the source property names and value types, changing their requiredness to optional.
A value may contain no source properties, one property, or any larger subset of the source shape.
Partial is a predefined transformation rather than an application-specific helper that must be declared locally.
No import is needed before using Partial in a TypeScript project.
gotchas: Partial<T> permits an empty object as well as any combination of the source type’s properties; it does not require at least one field.

interview.question: What does the TypeScript paths option do?
interview.answer: The paths option declares custom import-resolution mappings. Its keys can represent an import name or prefix, and the values are lookup locations resolved relative to baseUrl when present, otherwise relative to tsconfig.json.
interview.followUp: Does paths make Node.js understand the alias? No. The page explicitly says emitted import paths are unchanged, so the runtime or bundler needs its own mapping.

interview.question: How do wildcard paths mappings work?
interview.answer: Each mapping associates an import pattern with one or more target patterns. For example, app/* can map to ./src/app/*, allowing imports such as app/config to be checked against src/app/config.
interview.followUp: Why might multiple targets be useful? They provide fallback lookup locations when the first target does not resolve.

interview.question: How are paths targets located, and what is its relationship to baseUrl?
interview.answer: When baseUrl is set, path targets are interpreted relative to that directory. Without baseUrl, they are interpreted relative to the tsconfig file itself; since TypeScript 4.1, baseUrl is not required for paths.
interview.followUp: What must be configured outside TypeScript? The tool that loads or bundles the code must reproduce the mapping because tsc does not rewrite these imports.

If baseUrl is absent, target paths are resolved from the directory containing the tsconfig file.
The option affects TypeScript's resolution of require and import specifiers during analysis.
An exact mapping can make a bare import resolve to a local vendor file while preserving the convenient import name.
Wildcard aliases provide project-specific prefixes for locating source modules.
gotchas: paths does not rewrite emitted JavaScript imports, so the runtime, loader, or bundler must independently understand the same alias.
Do not treat paths as a runtime alias configuration; pair it with matching tooling.

interview.answer: Pick<Type, Keys> creates a type containing only the properties listed by Keys from Type. Keys can be a string literal or a union of string literals.
interview.followUp: How would you select several fields? Use a union such as Pick<User, "id" | "name">, which retains both properties.

interview.question: Why use Pick instead of declaring a second object type?
interview.answer: It is useful when a larger model contains more data than a particular API response or component should expose. The resulting type is derived from the original type rather than rewritten manually.
interview.followUp: What maintenance benefit follows? Changes to the selected properties in the source type flow into the picked type.

interview.question: How is Pick declared and made available?
interview.answer: Pick is available globally as a TypeScript utility type, so it does not require an import. Its documented form is Pick<Type, Keys>.
interview.followUp: When was it introduced? The documentation marks Pick as released in TypeScript 2.1.

readonly.summary: The readonly property modifier lets an object property be assigned during initialization but prevents later assignments through that property. It is a compile-time, shallow protection rather than runtime deep immutability.
readonly.explanation: Prefix an interface property with readonly to make it assignable when the object is created but not writable afterward through that property. This restriction is enforced by TypeScript’s type system, so it does not make the referenced value deeply immutable or alter runtime behavior.

interview.question: What does readonly do to an interface property?
interview.answer: readonly is a property modifier that prevents assignments to that property during type-checking after initialization. It is appropriate for object properties whose value should not be replaced by consumers.
interview.followUp: Does readonly create runtime immutability? No. It is a compile-time restriction and does not change JavaScript runtime behavior.

interview.question: How does readonly differ from const?
interview.answer: const applies to variables, while readonly applies to properties. A const variable cannot be rebound, whereas a readonly property cannot be assigned through that property after creation.
interview.followUp: Can a readonly property hold mutable data? Yes; the property reference cannot be replaced, but the referenced value may still be changed unless its own type prevents mutation.

interview.question: Does readonly make an object deeply immutable?
interview.answer: A readonly property is shallow: it blocks rewriting the property itself but does not recursively freeze nested objects. Use readonly array or tuple types when the collection’s mutating operations should be unavailable through that reference.
interview.followUp: What type represents an array that should not be mutated? ReadonlyArray<T> provides an array view with mutating methods removed.

keyPoints: Readonly properties express that an object’s selected fields may be set during creation but should not be changed afterward.
In an interface, place readonly before the property name in its declaration.
Once a readonly object property has been initialized, later assignments to it are rejected by the type checker.
ReadonlyArray<T> exposes array contents without mutation methods such as push, pop, or splice.
gotchas: Use const for variables and readonly for properties; they apply to different declarations.

Readonly.summary: Readonly<Type> creates a type whose properties cannot be reassigned by TypeScript. It is useful for describing frozen or otherwise read-only object views.
Readonly.explanation: Readonly<Type> creates a mapped type whose properties correspond to Type but are marked readonly. TypeScript therefore rejects assignments to those properties, making the type useful for values such as frozen objects; this restriction applies during type-checking rather than enforcing runtime immutability.

parameters.name: Type
parameters.description: The source object type whose properties become readonly.

Readonly.returns: A type with all properties of Type marked readonly.

interview.question: What does Readonly<T> do?
interview.answer: Readonly<Type> constructs a type with every property of Type marked readonly. Assignments to those properties are rejected by the type checker.
interview.followUp: How would you type a freezing helper? Use a generic signature such as function freeze<Type>(obj: Type): Readonly<Type>;.

interview.question: When is Readonly<T> useful?
interview.answer: It is useful when modeling an object whose properties cannot be reassigned, including the result type of a frozen-object helper. The restriction is represented statically by the readonly properties.
interview.followUp: What does it not guarantee? It does not by itself perform the runtime operation that freezes the object.

interview.question: When was Readonly<T> introduced and how is it characterized?
interview.answer: The utility was released in TypeScript 2.1. Its behavior is expressed through a mapped type that applies readonly to each property in the input type.
interview.followUp: What related array type should be considered? ReadonlyArray<T> is the dedicated type for arrays that should not be mutated.

keyPoints: Readonly<T> preserves the input type's property set while changing each property to readonly.
The resulting properties cannot receive new values through ordinary assignments accepted by the type checker.
A generic freeze-style function can expose its input as Readonly<Type> in the return type.
The utility is representable as a mapped type iterating over keyof T and retaining each property's value type.
gotchas: Readonly<T> describes the type-level restriction; it does not itself freeze an object or guarantee runtime immutability.

Record.summary: Record<Keys, Type> constructs an object type whose keys come from Keys and whose values all use Type. It is useful for strongly typed dictionaries and lookup tables.
Record.explanation: Record<Keys, Type> creates an object type with one property for every key in Keys, assigning Type as the value type for each property. It is useful when a known set of property names must all share a value shape.

interview.question: What does Record<K, T> represent?
interview.answer: Record<K, T> describes an object whose keys are K and whose values are T. If K is a union, each member becomes a required property in the resulting object type.
interview.followUp: How does Record differ from a mapped type over an existing type? Record creates properties from its key type rather than copying properties and their modifiers from an input type.

interview.question: How can Record enforce a complete lookup table?
interview.answer: A union such as "home" | "about" | "contact" constrains the permitted property names. The value type is applied uniformly to every one of those properties.
interview.followUp: What happens when a key is omitted from an object assigned to Record<K, T>? The assignment fails because the mapped key set requires that property.

interview.question: When was Record introduced and where is it available?
interview.answer: Record is globally available as a TypeScript utility type and was released in TypeScript 2.1. It is intended for common object-type transformations and does not require an import.
interview.followUp: When would an index signature be less precise? An index signature can allow arbitrary keys, whereas Record with a literal-key union restricts the object to the declared key set.

keyPoints: Record<Keys, Type> maps a key type to a common value type, producing an object type with those properties.
It is useful for expressing dictionaries and lookup tables whose entries share a defined value shape.
A generic Record can preserve a known key set while transforming each value from one type to another.

Required.summary: Required<Type> transforms an object type so all of its properties are required. It is the inverse counterpart to Partial<Type>.
Required.explanation: Required<Type> creates a new object type from Type in which optional properties are treated as required. It changes the type-level property modifiers, so values assigned to the resulting type must include every property that Type declares.

interview.question: What does Required<Type> do?
interview.answer: Required<Type> constructs a type whose properties are all required. For an interface with optional members, assigning an object to Required<Interface> requires values for every member.
interview.followUp: How does Required differ from NonNullable? NonNullable removes null and undefined from a type, whereas Required changes property optionality.

interview.question: Does Required fill in missing runtime properties?
interview.answer: It operates on the properties declared by Type and removes their optional property modifier. It does not create runtime defaults or insert missing values into an object.
interview.followUp: What happens at runtime? Nothing: Required is erased during compilation, so validation or defaulting must be implemented separately.

interview.question: When was Required introduced and where is it available?
interview.answer: Required was released in TypeScript 2.8 and is available as a global utility type. Its purpose is to make all properties of the supplied type required.
interview.followUp: Why is it useful in a large codebase? It can express a completed configuration or normalized object after a separate construction step.

keyPoints: The utility produces a transformed object type where every property from the input type is required.
Required can be used without importing it from a package.
It provides the inverse property-optional transformation of Partial.
An object omitting a formerly optional member is rejected when assigned to the Required version.
gotchas: Required reverses Partial's effect: it requires properties that Partial would make optional.

interview.question: What does ReturnType do, and how is it commonly used?
interview.answer: ReturnType<Type> constructs a type from the return type of a function type. For a named function value, use ReturnType<typeof fn> so typeof supplies its function type.
interview.followUp: What happens with an overloaded function? ReturnType infers from the last signature, which is generally the catch-all overload.

interview.question: Does ReturnType execute a function?
interview.answer: It is a type-level utility, so it does not call the function or change runtime behavior. It reuses the function's declared or inferred result type elsewhere in the program.
interview.followUp: How can you obtain the return type of an inline function type? Write ReturnType<() => Result>, or use a compatible function type directly.

interview.question: When was ReturnType introduced?
interview.answer: The utility was released in TypeScript 2.8. It is globally available as one of TypeScript's predefined utility types.
interview.followUp: Which related utility extracts a constructor's instance type? InstanceType performs that analogous operation for constructor functions.

keyPoints: It creates a type alias for whatever result type the supplied function type produces.
ReturnType has been available since TypeScript 2.8.
No import is needed because ReturnType is globally available.
Overload inference is based on the final call signature.
Its overload behavior is connected to conditional-type inference rules.
gotchas: With overloads, ReturnType uses the final signature rather than selecting a return type from the particular call.

satisfies.summary: The satisfies operator checks that an expression conforms to a target type without changing the expression’s inferred type. It catches structural mistakes while preserving precise property and method inference.
satisfies.explanation: The postfix satisfies operator checks that an expression conforms to a target type, but leaves the expression's inferred type intact. This combines structural validation—such as detecting missing or misspelled properties—with precise property access and method inference afterward.

interview.question: What problem does the satisfies operator solve?
interview.answer: satisfies checks whether an expression is compatible with a type, while preserving the expression's own inferred type. This lets TypeScript report structural mistakes without losing specific property information.
interview.followUp: How would you retain tuple information in a validated configuration? Use satisfies with a target containing the tuple type, allowing the original tuple inference to remain available.

interview.question: How does satisfies differ from a type annotation?
interview.answer: A type annotation can make a value conform to a broader type and thereby expose only that broader view. satisfies performs the compatibility check without changing the value's resulting type, so specific members and methods remain usable.
interview.followUp: Why can palette.green.toUpperCase() work in the documentation example? The property is inferred as the string literal value type rather than being reduced to the broader string-or-array union.

interview.question: What kinds of errors can satisfies catch?
interview.answer: In a record-like object, satisfies can detect an unknown key such as a misspelled color because every property must be compatible with the target mapping. At the same time, correctly typed properties keep their precise inferred forms.
interview.followUp: What happens if a required key is omitted? The expression fails validation because it does not satisfy the required record shape.

keyPoints: Use satisfies when an expression must conform to a design or configuration shape.
The operator preserves detailed inference, including property-specific types useful to later code.
It is a postfix operator placed after the expression and followed by the target type.
A mapped target such as Record<Colors, string | RGB> can validate every named property against an allowed value type.
It is useful for configuration objects where misspelled keys and incompatible values should be rejected.
gotchas: satisfies validates compatibility but does not replace the expression's inferred type with the target type.
It checks the expression against the target type, so incompatible properties or keys still produce errors.

interview.question: What does skipLibCheck do?
interview.answer: skipLibCheck is a compiler option that skips full type checking of declaration files. TypeScript still checks the application code and the declarations that code specifically refers to, which can reduce compilation time.
interview.followUp: What is the main risk? Errors caused by inconsistent declarations can be missed, so the setting reduces type-system accuracy.

interview.question: When might a large codebase use skipLibCheck?
interview.answer: It is useful when large declaration files dominate compilation or when dependency trees contain conflicting copies of a library’s types. The speed improvement comes from avoiding a complete check of all .d.ts files.
interview.followUp: What should be investigated first for duplicate types? Dependency resolution should be examined to ensure only one copy of the dependency is present.

interview.question: Why can skipLibCheck conceal real problems?
interview.answer: It should not automatically be treated as the permanent fix for duplicate or conflicting types. The documentation recommends resolving the dependency tree, and it also describes using the option temporarily during TypeScript-version migrations.
interview.followUp: How can standard-library declaration problems be addressed? TypeScript 4.5’s lib replacement technique can replace the affected standard library declarations.

keyPoints: The option suppresses full checking for declaration files, including files with the .d.ts extension.
TypeScript does not completely validate every declaration file when this setting is enabled.
Declarations reached through application source references still participate in checking.
Conflicting duplicate type definitions are a representative problem this setting can bypass.
A duplicated library type package in node_modules is a common reason teams consider enabling the option.
Problems originating in TypeScript’s standard-library declarations have a distinct remediation path.
gotchas: The option trades type-system accuracy for faster compilation, so errors inside skipped declarations may go undetected.
If duplicate library types exist in node_modules, prefer dependency-resolution remedies such as Yarn resolutions instead of relying on this option.
It can be a temporary migration aid when updated TypeScript or standard-library declarations create unwanted node_modules errors.

interview.question: What does the `sourceMap` option do?
interview.answer: `sourceMap` is a boolean compiler option that causes TypeScript to emit source-map files for generated JavaScript. The maps let debuggers and other tools show the original TypeScript while executing the emitted code.
interview.followUp: How can maps be embedded instead? Use `inlineSourceMap`, which puts the map content into the emitted JavaScript rather than writing a separate `.js.map` file.

interview.question: What files and metadata does enabling `sourceMap` produce?
interview.answer: With `sourceMap: true`, each emitted `.js` file has a neighboring `.js.map` or `.jsx.map` file. The JavaScript also contains a source-map comment that points external tools to that map.
interview.followUp: What related option maps declaration files? `declarationMap` emits maps for `.d.ts` files so navigation can lead back to the original TypeScript source.

interview.question: Why enable source maps in a large codebase?
interview.answer: The option is useful during debugging because it maps generated JavaScript locations to the original TypeScript source. It does not itself alter the runtime JavaScript behavior; it supplies debugging metadata.
interview.followUp: How can debugger source locations be customized? `sourceRoot` specifies a path or URL where the debugger should locate the TypeScript files.

The emitted maps let debugging tools present TypeScript locations instead of only generated JavaScript locations.
A separate map is produced beside the corresponding JavaScript output, using a `.js.map` or `.jsx.map` suffix.

interview.question: What does TypeScript's `strict` option do?
interview.answer: `strict` is a compiler setting that enables the strict mode family, providing stronger correctness guarantees. It is configured as a boolean compiler option in `tsconfig.json` or via the compiler command line.
interview.followUp: How would you adopt it incrementally? Enable `strict`, then explicitly disable individual strict-family options that currently block migration and remove those exceptions over time.

interview.question: Why is `strict` useful in a large codebase?
interview.answer: It enables the strict mode family as a group rather than requiring each family option to be listed separately. The resulting checks are intended to provide stronger guarantees of program correctness.
interview.followUp: Why can enabling it change compiler output diagnostics after an upgrade? The family can gain additional stricter checks in future TypeScript versions.

interview.question: Can individual strict checks be disabled while `strict` is enabled?
interview.answer: `strict` does not prevent targeted configuration: individual strict-family checks can be turned off after enabling the umbrella option. This supports staged migrations while preserving the other strict checks.
interview.followUp: What should a team review after upgrading TypeScript? Recompile and assess newly reported errors, including errors caused by stricter behavior added under `strict`.

keyPoints: It is an umbrella compiler flag that activates a broad collection of stricter type-checking behavior.
Its purpose is to increase the compiler's guarantees about program correctness.
Enabling it is equivalent to enabling every option in TypeScript's strict-mode family.
gotchas: A TypeScript upgrade can introduce new errors because newer strict checks may be added to this option.
The umbrella setting is not all-or-nothing: override a specific strict-family option if necessary.

strictFunctionTypes.explanation: The strictFunctionTypes compiler option makes function-parameter comparison contravariant instead of bivariant. It prevents assigning a callback that accepts only a narrower type to a callback type that may pass a broader type; method and constructor declarations remain exempt.
